articles.title: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats during West Bank olive harvest
articles.text:
Israeli settlers attack European diplomats during West Bank olive harvest | Israel-Palestine conflict News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
An Israeli soldier fires a tear gas grenade toward Palestinian olive pickers during the olive harvest on October 17, 2026 in Abu Falah, West Bank [Faiz Abu Rmeleh/Getty Images]
By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and AP
Published On 17 Oct 202617 Oct 2026
Israeli settlers have attacked European diplomats, including a French mayor, near the Palestinian village of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank.
The delegation was visiting Palestinian olive harvesters on Saturday when the Israeli attackers confronted the group. The attack comes a day after settlers assaulted an American journalist north of Ramallah.
In Saturday’s incident, the settlers targeted Belgium’s consul general, French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives, Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said.
“A French mayor was assaulted and a Belgian vehicle damaged,” Prevot said, linking the attack to what he called Israel’s “illegal settlement policy” and pledged to push for further European Union sanctions.
French mayor Bernard Baudoux, who was assaulted, told the AFP news agency that the violence suggests that “there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government” towards settler violence.
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah, said the settlers surrounded the diplomats’ vehicles, pelted them with stones and smashed their windows.
Taybeh’s mayor told Al Jazeera the settlers blocked the diplomats’ vehicles, assaulted members of the group and shattered a window.
The assault has prompted an Israeli police investigation and condemnation from Belgium as settler attacks disrupt the harvest across the occupied territory.
Settler attacks continue
Earlier on Saturday, several Palestinians were injured by Israeli settlers, as Israeli forces arrested farmers during pogroms across the occupied West Bank.
Advertisement
Four women and a child were among six people injured when Israeli settlers attacked residents in Ma’in village in the Masafer Yatta area, south of Hebron, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS).
In the town of Deir Ammar, west of Ramallah, Israeli forces opened fire on farmers picking olives, forcing them to leave their land, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
In the same area, Israeli settlers shot and injured two Palestinians. In the village of Tuqu, southeast of Bethlehem, Israeli forces fired on a Palestinian civilian vehicle.
In the village of Kafr Malek, northeast of Ramallah, settlers raided a farm at dawn and killed about 20 sheep, Mayor Najeh Rustum told Al Jazeera.
He added that Israeli forces had raided the village the previous night as well, firing tear gas canisters that ignited a fire in a house and caused material damage.
‘Part of a campaign’
Al Jazeera’s Odeh said settlers destroyed olive trees across the Beit Furik plain, east of Nablus, in the northern West Bank while Israeli forces arrested landowners and olive pickers.
In the village of Deir Jarir, east of Ramallah, she said, settlers under army protection fired live ammunition at farmers in the al-Hariq area to prevent them from completing the harvest and forced them off their land.
Settlers also smashed the vehicle of international activist Jonathan Budlak in the village and threw stones at a farmer’s vehicle.
In the village of Burqa near Ramallah, Israeli forces and settlers prevented farmers from picking olives, Odeh said, adding that settlers attacked farmers in the Wadi al-Sha’er area, southeast of Salfit.
“What we see, whether it’s in Beit Furik, Kafr Malek, Deir Jarir or elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, is part of a campaign,” Odeh said.
She said settlers have become increasingly emboldened, publicly advertising attack campaigns on social media platforms.
“There have been 300 documented attacks since the beginning of October, and that has had a devastating impact on a very important season for Palestinian farmers,” she said, adding that danger comes from soldiers and settlers alike as military forces routinely intervene to protect settlers and attack Palestinians defending their land.
A settler throws a stone towards Palestinians in Abu Falah near Ramallah on October 16, 2026, during attacks carried out as Palestinians try to harvest olives [Ammar Awad/Reuters]
Prominent rabbi justifies attacks
The attacks follow a religious edict issued by Rabbi Dov Lior, a prominent rabbi for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party and a leading authority among the Hilltop Youth, which is a religious Zionist group devoted to seizing Palestinian land in the West Bank.
Advertisement
In the edict, Lior stated that harvesting olives in the Holy Land is entirely permitted and carries an added virtue, given security dangers.
He wrote that Jews are permitted to harvest olives even in areas far from Jewish communities to publicly display ownership of the land and fulfil God’s commandment of conquering it. He claimed the land belongs to the Jewish people and Palestinians did not buy or rent it.
Odeh said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu downplays pogroms and no concrete action is taken to stop them.
“It is a matter of debate among politicians, but no one is stopping these settlers, whose names, locations and homes are known,” she said, adding that politicians permit the violence to continue because “it is politically expedient” and secures votes before elections on October 27.
Advertisement

articles.title: Tens of thousands protest for reforms in France amid tear gas and unrest
articles.text:
Tens of thousands protest for reforms in France amid tear gas and unrest | Protests News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
The monument at Place de la Republique wears a 'yellow vest' as clashes erupt during a protest in Paris, France on October 17, 2026 as part of a nationwide call for mobilisation [AFP]
By Virginia Pietromarchi
Published On 17 Oct 202617 Oct 2026
Paris, France – Marianne, the statue personifying of the French Republic, towers over Place de la Republique in Paris, wearing a yellow vest.
At the base of the monument, the faces of the three allegorical figures representing Liberty, Equality and Fraternity are streaked with black tears. Above them, tear gas canisters arc through the air, filling the square with smoke.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 France’s mounting debt: Is Europe next?
list 2 of 3 Protests spread across France as ‘yellow vests’ set to join
list 3 of 3 France tackles new wave of nationwide protestsend of list
This was the scene as tens of thousands of protesters, mostly young people, rallied at the heart of the French capital on Saturday in the latest act of a movement that has been rocking France to the core for more than a month now, demanding better education and a fairer system.
“Everybody has come together asking the government for a final time to hear us loud and clear because it is not OK what is happening,” said a high school student who asked not to be identified, her fist raised in the air.
“We are here because we want to take back our rights,” she said.
The movement, hailed by some as a historical social movement, has gained cross-class, cross-working sector support, uniting groups including remnants of the “ yellow vest” movement – the grassroots cost-of-living protests that shook France in 2018.
The presence of nurses, human rights lawyers, firefighters, parents, teachers and some remnants of the “yellow vests” on Saturday was a testament to how pupils have catalysed a social discontent running deep across French society.
The CGT, one of France’s major labour unions, also backed the protests, calling for “higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people’s needs”.
Advertisement
The union said more than 500,000 people protested across the country on Saturday.
‘Young people are anxious’
A recurring theme among protesters interviewed by Al Jazeera was that the system has failed them, violence is used too casually, and that any prospect of a better future looks bleak.
Anxiety was a recurring word.
“Young people are anxious about their futures and their failing schools; the yellow vests are distressed by the cost of living, which is literally exploding; and there are existential anxieties regarding the geopolitical situation,” said Jean Pierre, a member of the French Human Rights League. “That is why there are so many people out there; it is the result of a whole host of anxieties that people are feeling today,”
Parents were also present. Amelie, a mother of three, did not want to provide her last name. With eyes tickling over the smell of tear gas, she said it was important for her to support them.
“We will keep up the pressure to make sure someone is taking care of our children’s future,” she said, while standing next to her teen daughter.
At each corner of the square, there was a heavy police presence of large numbers of riot police officers dressed in full gear.
Gas canisters were launched in the early hours of the protest at noon despite a scarce presence of people. Yet, from 2pm onwards (12:00 GMT), the square was packed, and it became tense.
Clashes broke out between the police and some of the protesters, who threw firework mortars at officers and set one car and a newspaper stand on fire, sending a thick cloud of black smoke up into the sky.
The smell of tear gas could be felt from streets away, as well as the sound of what seemed like sound grenades that became more frequent as the day progressed.
Coffee shops and boutiques closed for the day as the sound of firefighters’ sirens crossed the city. Still, the vast majority of the protesters peacefully joined the march that started moving towards northwestern Paris.
Protesters, police and water cannons are seen during a demonstration to protest against the ‘high cost of living’, at Place de la Republique in Paris on October 17, 2026 [AFP]
Elsewhere in France, in the southern city of Marseille, demonstrators breached the town hall and looted shops; in Lyon media reports said a tourism office was set ablaze.
France’s Ministry of the Interior said that by 3pm (13:00 GMT) some 272 people had been arrested after violent incidents involving hooded individuals, including in Paris, Marseille in the south, Rennes in the northwest, Toulouse in the southwest and Angers in the west.
Advertisement
“Such actions include attempted looting, confrontations with law enforcement, the setting ⁠of fires to street furniture and the targeting of seats of power and media outlets,” it said, blaming the unrest on what it described as the “ultra-left”.
Bruno Cautres, a researcher at the Paris-based Center for Political Research, told Al Jazeera that Saturday’s events are the “culmination of different mobilisations” that emerged out of frustrations about high taxes combined with a significant national debt and deficit that is preventing the government from satisfying public demands.
“The French are asking themselves where are we going as a country? How are we going to get out of this budget crisis?” Cautres said.
No easy way out
The protests began in mid-September at a high school in the Paris suburb of Creteil, where students took to the streets over dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and what they see as a deeply unequal education system.
Saturday’s mobilisation followed calls on social media to revive the “yellow vests” movement, which emerged in 2018 against diesel prices but quickly morphed into a movement against President Emmanuel M

articles.title: Egypt’s Sisi seeks authorisation for defence assistance to Saudi Arabia
articles.text:
Egypt’s Sisi seeks authorisation for defence assistance to Saudi Arabia | Abdel Fattah el-Sisi News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Egyptian President Abdel Fatah el-Sisi with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Cairo, September 15, 2026 [Bandar Algaloud/Saudi Royal Court/Reuters]
By Al Jazeera Staff
Published On 17 Oct 202617 Oct 2026
Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has called for an emergency parliamentary session to authorise him to approve any requests from Saudi Arabia for defence assistance, if Riyadh were to ask.
Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy on Saturday, el-Sisi emphasised Cairo’s readiness to back the kingdom.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Trump eases Russia oil sanctions, but is Europe still buying Moscow’s gas?
list 2 of 3 Protests spread across France as ‘yellow vests’ set to join
list 3 of 3 Israeli settlers attack European diplomats during West Bank olive harvestend of list
Egypt will “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia “in accordance with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and the directives of the Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman”, he said.
“I know that this matter requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I hope that parliament will convene in an emergency session to give us this authorisation, if it is requested of us,” he said.
“I am not speaking in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone. I am speaking only for defence.”
Attacks on Saudi Arabia
The request follows a barrage of attacks on the kingdom from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, including airports and oil facilities.
Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of the capital, Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport earlier this month killed 14 people and wounded more than 300. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Dammam, Abha, Jazan and Najran.
Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government launched a full-scale military campaign against the Houthis this month to recapture territory seized by them.
Advertisement
El-Sisi had backed Saudi calls for secure and unhindered navigation in the Red Sea in a meeting with the Saudi Crown Prince, known as MBS, in Cairo last month.
A statement from the Egyptian presidency then said that “the security of Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states is an integral part of Egypt’s national security”.
Red Sea security
That meeting came just days after the Houthis seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, gaining significant control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal.
Saudi Arabia already has a defence pact with Pakistan and Turkiye, known as the Mecca Alliance for Defence, which was signed in August.
Earlier this month, the three countries agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under the pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.
Analysts say Riyadh is looking for help to protect the kingdom and Red Sea shipping and that Egypt, whose Suez Canal revenue depends on the same traffic, is an obvious partner.
They say Egypt is eager to prevent Iran and its allies from imposing control over the region, especially over maritime traffic in the Red Sea, given the direct repercussions for the Suez Canal.
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging Houthi attacks against the kingdom, a claim Tehran rejects. Iran has offered assistance to halt the conflict between the two sides.
Sisi’s future
Speaking to recruits at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital on Saturday, el-Sisi also confirmed that he would not seek to extend his presidency beyond 2030, in line with the Egyptian constitution.
“The period leading up to 2030 will be the end of my term as president of the state, if I am still alive,” he said.
He added that his decision is “completely settled” and there will be “no discussion” about it.
Egypt’s constitution was updated in 2019 to increase term length to six years from four, and to allow el-Sisi to run for another six-year term in 2023. That means his term is due to expire in 2030, and he is not allowed to run again.
He said the Egyptian constitution “would not be touched”.
Advertisement

articles.title: Thousands rally for biggest protest in years against Tunisia’s Saied
articles.text:
Thousands rally for biggest protest in years against Tunisia’s Saied | Protests News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Tunisians joined the latest protest on Saturday against President Kais Saied and the high cost of living [Zoubeir Souissi/Reuters]
By AFP and Reuters
Published On 17 Oct 202617 Oct 2026
Thousands of Tunisians have marched through the capital to protest against President Kais Saied, worsening living conditions and restrictions on political freedoms.
The latest demonstration in Tunis on Saturday was led by the Tunisian General Labour Union (UGTT), an influential trade union federation, alongside opposition parties and civil society organisations.
Recommended Stories list of 2 items
list 1 of 2 Tunisia: What has Kais Saied achieved economically in seven years?
list 2 of 2 Tunisia softens its ‘false news’ penalty. What really changed, and why now?end of list
It was the largest protest against Saied in years, bringing together political opponents whose longstanding divisions have weakened their ability to challenge his rule.
The AFP news agency reported that more than 3,000 people were on the march, but the total could not be independently confirmed.
Protesters gathered along Habib Bourguiba Avenue, a major street in central Tunis, as hundreds of police deployed across the capital. Several surrounding roads were closed.
The crowd included lawyers, doctors, journalists and the unemployed, as well as activists and members of parties from across the political spectrum. They demanded the release of detained government critics and an end to restrictions on trade union rights.
Placards reading “No democracy without freedoms” and “No dignity with poverty” reflected the political and economic grievances driving the demonstration.
Tunisian General Labour Union (UGTT) Secretary-General Salah Eddine Salmi and other demonstrators protest against President Kais Saied in Tunis on Saturday [Zoubeir Souissi/Reuters]
Protesters also revived a slogan demanding the government’s removal, widely heard during Tunisia’s 2011 uprising.
Advertisement
Addressing the rally on Saturday, UGTT leader Salah Eddine Salmi criticised the concentration of political power in the presidency and said “silence will no longer be acceptable”.
The political demands came alongside mounting frustration over the cost of basic goods and declining purchasing power.
Prolonged difficulties
Tunisia has struggled with prolonged economic difficulties, deteriorating public services, recurring water and electricity cuts, as well as shortages of medicines and other essentials.
Demonstrator Yassine Gharseli, who travelled from Sfax, about 250km south of Tunis, said repeated disruptions to basic services had deepened his frustration with the authorities.
“I came from Sfax to stand up for my freedom,” he told the Reuters news agency at the demo, expressing his determination to continue speaking out.
Saturday’s march followed other demonstrations over similar grievances.
On August 20 , protesters in Tunis rallied against rising prices and shortages of basic goods.
Last month, fuel transport workers went on a two-day strike over wages and working conditions, led by a union federation affiliated with the UGTT.
The latest protest over economic hardship and restrictions on freedoms in Tunis on Saturday [Zoubeir Souissi/Reuters]
The demands recall the uprising that ousted longtime President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali in 2011, which helped ignite protests across the Arab world.
Tunisia subsequently held competitive elections and expanded political freedoms, but unemployment and struggling public services remain persistent sources of anger.
Saied came to power promising an alternative to that political system; however, in 2021, he suspended parliament and dismissed the government, saying he was confronting corruption and political deadlock.
He later dissolved parliament and a new constitution increased presidential powers in 2022.
Advertisement

articles.title: Why Trump’s latest White House press secretary lasted just five days
articles.text:
Why Trump’s latest White House press secretary lasted just five days | Donald Trump News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
US President Donald Trump, joined by White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, prepares to speak to reporters as he departs the White House, in Washington, DC, US, October 13 [Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA]
By Al Jazeera Staff
Published On 17 Oct 202617 Oct 2026
United States President Donald Trump’s latest press secretary has been let go after just five days on the job, following a widely criticised first – and only – White House news conference and amid scrutiny of her credentials.
Trump told reporters on Friday that he believed the press had been harsh towards his new top spokesperson, Katie Zacharia, but that he had advised her to “reconsider” the role.
Shortly after, Al Jazeera and other media confirmed that Zacharia would be “ transitioning out” of the position.
That made her the shortest-serving press secretary in US history – even shorter than the tenure of Anthony Scaramucci, the former White House communications director who was fired after 10 days on the job during Trump’s first term in office in 2017.
His sacking gave rise to the term “one Scaramucci” – or “a Mooch” – which journalists and White House observers use jokingly as a measure of time to predict how long Trump officials would last in their jobs. Now, a new unit of time – “one Zacharia” – is only half as long.
Recalling his own White House stint this week, Scaramucci wrote on X: “Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”
Here’s what we know about Zacharia’s brief tenure:
Why was Katie Zacharia removed as White House press secretary?
The White House has not given an official reason for Zacharia’s departure, but it came amid mounting concerns about her competency and professional background.
During her first and only news conference on Tuesday, Zacharia appeared uneasy at the podium and struggled at times to get through her sentences. She fumbled her words while looking down at her notes, once confused the words “husband” and “president” and ended the briefing after 14 minutes, taking only three questions from reporters.
Advertisement
Scrutiny intensified after it emerged that Zacharia, who has a law degree and described herself as “an attorney”, had studied law at university but never passed the bar exam required to practice law in the US. She later claimed she had worked as a lawyer in China.
Conservative Fox News host Sean Hannity asked Zacharia during an awkward interview on Thursday: “Why didn’t you just say: ‘I never practised law’?”
Following news of her departure, Zacharia wrote on X that it had been “an honour” to work for Trump, calling him a “kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man”.
How was her one White House briefing received?
Zacharia, who took over from former press secretary Karoline Leavitt, was widely criticised as unpolished and unprepared during her appearance before the White House press corps on Tuesday this week, even by many of Trump’s allies.
During Hannity’s interview with Zacharia, he noted that she had been “widely panned” for her performance.
Conservative journalist and commentator Megyn Kelly said Zacharia needed “to present as a serious person”.
Jen Psaki, a former White House press secretary who worked under Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, compared Zacharia’s troubled briefing to a comedy skit. “Maybe this whole White House press secretary thing isn’t really for Katie,” she said. “It’s not for everybody.”
As a fellow White House deportee, Scaramucci gave Zacharia some advice. “Speaking as the world’s leading expert on short White House tenures: turn off the news and go enjoy your family. In time you’ll realize that the Universe did you a major favor,” he wrote on X.
Who will take over White House press briefings now?
That remains to be seen.
The White House has not announced a permanent replacement, and Trump told Fox News he is “not in a hurry” to fill the role.
The vacancy leaves Trump without a top spokesperson as the US remains mired in a conflict with Iran and heads into crucial midterm elections next month.
How many press secretaries has Trump gone through?
Zacharia was the sixth person to serve as White House press secretary under Trump. He went through four of the officials during his first term and, so far, two in his second.
Zacharia’s predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, had held the position since the start of Trump’s second term in January 2025. She resigned in August to spend more time with her children.
Trump’s first-term press secretaries were Kayleigh McEnany, Stephanie Grisham, Sarah Huckabee Sanders and Sean Spicer.
Advertisement
McEnany and Spicer now work in media. McEnany hosts several shows on Fox News, while Spicer contributing to NewsNation and has launched his own podcast.
Huckabee Sanders currently serves as the governor of her home state of Arkansas, where she is seeking re-election on November 3.
Grisham left the press secretary position after less than a year in 2020 and became First Lady Melania Trump’s chief of staff. She resigned that role after the January 6, 2021 insurrection and has since become a major critic of the US president.
Which other Trump-appointed officials have been fired?
Zacharia joins a roll call of Trump administration officials to be pushed out during his second term.
Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece who was previously engaged to Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr, was asked to step down from her role earlier this week after reports emerged that she offered a political donor access to senior administration officials in exchange for money.
US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle presents her credentials at the presidential palace, in Athens, Greece, November 4 [File: Louisa Gouliamaki/Reuters]
Earlier in the year, Trump fired Attorney General Pam Bondi amid controversy over her handling of files relating to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, which h

articles.title: Hardline Israeli rabbi ruling on stolen Palestinian olives prompts uproar
articles.text:
Hardline Israeli rabbi ruling on stolen Palestinian olives prompts uproar | Israel-Palestine conflict News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Rabbi Dov Lior (C) attends a rally near the Supreme court in Jerusalem on July 4, 2011, against his and another rabbi, Yaacov Yosef''s, brief arrest. Israeli police recently detained the leading rabbis after they ignored a police summons to be questioned over endorsements for The King''s Doctrine, a book written by a more obscure settler rabbi offering justifications from scripture for killing innocent gentiles during religious war [Ronen Zvulun/Reuters]
By Mohammad Mansour
Published On 17 Oct 202617 Oct 2026
Prominent Israeli Rabbi Dov Lior issued a Jewish religious ruling on Friday permitting settlers to steal olives from Palestinian orchards in the occupied West Bank.
Lior’s ruling claims that Palestinian landowners who could not access their olives during the harvest season due to Israeli restrictions have been sufficiently compensated in the years they had access to the fruit. According to the ruling, Jews are permitted to pick these olives to claim ownership of the Palestinian land.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Palestinians, US journalist attacked in West Bank pogrom: What we know
list 2 of 3 Jerusalem Daily: Israeli settlers burn Palestinian olive groves
list 3 of 3 Israeli raids and arrests in southern Syria push population to the brinkend of list
Lior, born in Poland in 1933, went as far as classifying the theft of olives from Palestinian farms as an “additional virtue”, as settler pogroms and Israeli occupation continue in the West Bank.
He added that settlers should “conquer the land” far from Jewish communities in order to publicly “demonstrate our ownership” and follow biblical commandment.
“The Jewish people have never given up on the Land of Israel, as we express in our prayers every single day,” the ruling continues. “The Arabs never purchased the land from the Jewish people or from any individual Jew, and therefore it is stolen land in their hands… They never bought it in any way and it remained under the ownership of the Jewish people.”
The olive press in the town of Qusra operates on the first day of the olive harvest season on October 9, 2026 in Nablus, West Bank [Faiz Abu Rmeleh/Getty Images]
Harvest violence
The ruling coincides with another wave of settler pogroms against Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest season. On Friday. at least 19 people were injured in 34 attacks by the Israeli military and settlers on Palestinians harvesting their crops across the West Bank.
Advertisement
An American photojournalist working for The Washington Post was assaulted by settlers while covering the daily violence, and five vehicles were torched.
Many Palestinian farmers have been unable to access their crops due to Israeli restrictions and the dangers from the settlers.
While settler pogroms are not exceptional, they come weeks before Israeli elections, with a push by far-right parties to gain the support of settlers and their supporters. But not all Jewish religious leaders backed the call to steal Palestinian olives.
Religious backlash
Rabbis from the religious council of the Gush Etzion settlements published a letter calling the illegal harvesting of Palestinian crops theft, blasphemy, and a moral defect.
Tzohar, an organisation of 800 orthodox rabbis, said in a statement that only the state has the authority to confiscate property. As long as the state recognises Arab ownership of the olives, they belong to them, it added.
Mamoun Abu Amer, an analyst on Israeli politics, told Al Jazeera that there could be political reasons behind the religious groups’ rejection of Rabbi Dov Lior’s comments.
“The position of the other rabbis who rejected this call might be a move driven by political motive and pressure from entities within the government to give the impression that these are anomalous voices that do not represent the general opinion of the settlers.
“The Israeli government is trying to portray that those who carry out these riots are a limited-number group that does not represent public opinion in the settlements, and that the settlers are peaceful, good, and law-abiding, and that the issue is confined to the ‘ Hilltop Youth‘ boys who commit these crimes,” he explained.
Rabbi Dov Lior holds immense influence among hardline settler groups, such as the Hilltop Youth, who fiercely back his hardline religious decrees that oppose any territorial compromise with Palestinians.
He is also a prominent figure within Israel’s Religious Zionist movement and serves as the spiritual guide for the far-right Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
“Ben-Gvir relies on the religious rulings of Rabbi Dov Lior, which rely on biblical texts and the Book of Deuteronomy,” Abu Amer noted. He claimed that Rabbi Lior adopts the most extreme interpretations in the Jewish religion.
“There is an important matter, which is that Ben-Gvir competes via the TikTok platform, propaganda, and populist rhetoric, and this is a rhetoric that serves him and brings him votes, given the environment and general atmosphere in Israel after the events of October 7, as there is a ‘market for extremism’ in the Israeli society,” Abu Amer added.

Knesset member Gilad Kariv of the left-wing Democrats Party criticised Lior, accusing him and his followers of dragging Israel into a flood of moral vice.
“Whoever stands on the sidelines in this issue joins the camp of Rabbi Dov Lior and his criminals,” Kariv said.

articles.title: US and Iran both claim control of Strait of Hormuz amid attacks on vessels
articles.text:
US and Iran both claim control of Strait of Hormuz amid attacks on vessels | Energy News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
A vessel transits the Gulf of Oman off the coast of Khor Fakkan in the emirate of Sharjah, eastern UAE, on October 13, 2026 [AFP]
By Maziar Motamedi
Published On 17 Oct 202617 Oct 2026
Tehran, Iran – Dozens of ships were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz in October as Iran and the United States compete to assert their authority over the waterway.
At least 12 ships were attacked in the week ending on October 16, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported late Friday, with one important caveat.

“UKMTO is struggling to accurately report true number of attacks with majority of vessels attacked refusing to report to UKMTO,” the maritime security organisation stated. It said it was aware of more incidents in the waterway via other sources but could not verify them due to a lack of information.
The same pattern has been true for the first half of October. The month has seen the highest number of ship attacks since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28.
Of the 12 vessels that were confirmed attacked, the organisation said half continued to their destination or reached port. One sank, two were disabled, and three were either damaged or had an unconfirmed outcome.
The UKMTO also reported a new type of attack on Saturday. The master of a tanker said their vessel was hit by a rocket-propelled grenade (RPG) fired from a small boat 78 nautical miles (equivalent to about 144km) northeast of Saudi Arabia’s city of Jubail, Eastern province, resulting in damage to the aft port quarter.
In recent months, the US has managed to increase energy transits through the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways through a shuttle system coordinated with Arab powers. But volumes have oscillated weekly due to rising Iranian attacks.
Advertisement
Oil flows through Hormuz were at 11.6 million barrels per day (bpd) over the seven days to October 13. This was about 68 percent of the 17.1 million bpd pre-war baseline, according to Kpler figures.
On Friday, Brent crude also touched $110 a barrel for the first time since May in light of ongoing attacks. The situation has been exacerbated by the Iran-aligned Houthis’ attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and their capture of the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Expectations that the conflict between the US and Iran was escalating have also impacted prices.
The US military has provided a starkly different outlook on the situation in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which accounted for roughly a fifth of global oil and natural gas flows before the war began.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) chief Brad Cooper claimed in a video message late Friday that despite the Iranian attacks, 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil moved through the Strait of Hormuz over the past week.
“Let me be clear: The Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran,” he said, attributing the greatly increased ship attacks to “desperation” by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The US military also claimed that it continues to prevent Iranian exports and imports via its southern ports through an “ironclad” naval blockade. It claims the blockade has cost Iran $25bn in oil export income, and that the US has recently seized $350m in Iranian cryptocurrency financing.
The UKMTO report said total outbound transit over the last seven days was 125 ships, with total inbound transits standing at 129. Over the week, most transits by the Western security agency were for dry bulk cargo, followed by tanker products and general cargo.
Tehran has not provided exact figures on how many vessels have been attacked, or how many are passing through the Hormuz, although it has said Washington is exaggerating numbers to project success of its naval campaign.
It comes as two vessels were reportedly hit by naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz this week, with the US and Iran offering contradictory claims about the situation.
The IRGC has increasingly reported that vessels are hitting mines across the strategic waterway, which it says remains unsafe for vessels which do not coordinate with Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority, an entity set up during the war to manage passage through the Hormuz.
The latest claim came on Saturday, when the IRGC said a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil caught fire after striking a mine while moving through an “unauthorised” route.
The Panama-flagged container shipping vessel Ten Neptune transits the Gulf of Oman off the coast of Khor Fakkan in the emirate of Sharjah, eastern UAE, on October 13, 2026 [AFP]
Iran’s state-run Press TV shared footage it says showed the tanker on fire. But CENTCOM said it had cleared the strait of naval mines, and that vessels are being struck by projectiles.
Advertisement
The latest incident “fact-checked” by the US military was on Thursday, when it said a civilian container ship, the M/V GFS Pride, was hit by an IRGC projectile, not by a mine as the Iranians had claimed. The vessel sank as it was being towed to shore.
The US has refrained from responding to any of the recent vessel attacks, but there are concerns that Washington could escalate the war after the November 3 midterm elections.
Diplomacy has not fully halted, with messages continuing to be relayed between the two parties by regional mediators like Pakistan, Qatar and others. But no breakthrough in talks is expected any time soon.
